title: Jeremiah 49:7–22
context: The LORD of Armies speaks through Jeremiah concerning Edom, the people descended from Esau (Genesis 36:1). He asks whether wisdom has vanished from Teman, commonly understood as a region or town in Edom, and warns the inhabitants of Dedan, commonly placed in northwest Arabia, to flee. Edom will be stripped bare beyond what grape gatherers or thieves would take, yet the LORD tells Edom to leave its fatherless children and widows to him, for he will preserve them. Edom too must drink the cup, a reference to the cup of wrath in 25:15–29, and the LORD swears that Bozrah, commonly identified as an Edomite city, will become a waste. Verses 14–16 and parts of verses 9–10 closely parallel Obadiah 1–9, which also speaks of news from the LORD, pride that deceives those who dwell in the clefts of the rock, and the eagle’s nest brought down; interpreters discuss the relationship between the two texts without agreement on which came first. Verse 18 compares Edom’s desolation to the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah (compare Genesis 19:24–25), and verses 19–21 reappear almost word for word in 50:44–46, applied there to Babylon. The unit ends with an enemy swooping like an eagle against Bozrah. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the oracle soberly, as shared ground about pride brought low and God’s rule over the nations.

verses.text: Of Edom, the LORD of Armies says: “Is wisdom no more in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent? Has their wisdom vanished?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD of Armies asking whether wisdom has vanished from Teman. Edom’s famed wisdom cannot save it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see human wisdom shown to be powerless before God’s purpose (compare Obadiah 1:8). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as humbling human cleverness.

verses.text: Flee! Turn back! Dwell in the depths, inhabitants of Dedan; for I will bring the calamity of Esau on him when I visit him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the inhabitants of Dedan told to flee and hide because the LORD will bring the calamity of Esau. The danger is near.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s visitation on Edom announced. Both traditions commonly read the verse in its historical setting, holding the location of Dedan with appropriate care.

verses.text: If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave some gleaning grapes? If thieves came by night, wouldn’t they steal until they had enough?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the image of grape gatherers and thieves, who would leave something behind. Edom’s loss will be more complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image shared with Obadiah 1:5. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober picture of thorough judgment.

verses.text: But I have made Esau bare, I have uncovered his secret places, and he will not be able to hide himself. His offspring is destroyed, with his brothers and his neighbors; and he is no more.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he has stripped Esau bare and uncovered his hiding places. Nothing can be concealed from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God exposing what Edom thought secure (compare Obadiah 1:6). Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, without dwelling on its severity.

verses.text: Leave your fatherless children. I will preserve them alive. Let your widows trust in me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying to leave the fatherless children with him, for he will preserve them, and to let the widows trust in him. Mercy appears even in judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s care for the vulnerable among the nations (compare Psalm 68:5; Psalm 146:9). Readers in both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about God’s compassion.

verses.text: For the LORD says: “Behold, they to whom it didn’t pertain to drink of the cup will certainly drink; and are you he who will altogether go unpunished? You won’t go unpunished, but you will surely drink.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying that even those who did not deserve the cup must drink, so Edom will not go unpunished. Justice is impartial.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cup imagery pointing back to 25:15–29. Both traditions commonly read the verse within that larger picture of God’s judgment on the nations.

verses.text: For I have sworn by myself,” says the LORD, “that Bozrah will become an astonishment, a reproach, a waste, and a curse. All its cities will be perpetual wastes.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD swearing by himself that Bozrah will become a waste and a reproach. His oath underscores certainty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s oath as a sign that his word will stand. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, holding the identification of Bozrah with care.

verses.text: I have heard news from the LORD, and an ambassador is sent among the nations, saying, “Gather yourselves together! Come against her! Rise up to the battle!”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the prophet saying he has heard news from the LORD and that an envoy summons the nations against Edom. God rallies the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God directing the movements of nations (compare Obadiah 1:1). Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the oracle’s announcement of judgment.

verses.text: “For, behold, I have made you small among the nations, and despised among men.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he has made Edom small and despised among the nations. Its former status among the nations is reversed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty over the rise and fall of peoples. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober statement of Edom’s humbling.

verses.text: As for your terror, the pride of your heart has deceived you, O you who dwell in the clefts of the rock, who hold the height of the hill, though you should make your nest as high as the eagle, I will bring you down from there,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Edom deceived by the pride of its heart, living in the clefts of the rock and nesting like an eagle, yet brought down by the LORD. Pride goes before a fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the warning against pride shared with Obadiah 1:3–4 (compare Proverbs 16:18). Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God humbling the proud.

verses.text: “Edom will become an astonishment. Everyone who passes by it will be astonished, and will hiss at all its plagues.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Edom becoming an astonishment, with passersby hissing at its plagues. Its fall will be widely seen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see judgment as a public witness. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, as part of the oracle’s picture of desolation.

verses.text: As in the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah and its neighbor cities,” says the LORD, “no man will dwell there, neither will any son of man live therein.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Edom’s desolation compared to the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah. No one will make a home there again.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the echo of Genesis 19:24–25, also used of Babylon in 50:40. Both traditions commonly read the comparison as a sober image of complete desolation.

verses.text: “Behold, he will come up like a lion from the pride of the Jordan against the strong habitation; for I will suddenly make them run away from it, and whoever is chosen, I will appoint him over it. For who is like me? Who will appoint me a time? Who is the shepherd who will stand before me?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see an attacker coming up like a lion from the thickets of the Jordan, and the LORD asking who is like him. No shepherd can stand before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s incomparable sovereignty. Readers in both traditions commonly note that these lines recur in 50:44 concerning Babylon.

verses.text: Therefore hear the counsel of the LORD, that he has taken against Edom, and his purposes that he has purposed against the inhabitants of Teman: Surely they will drag them away, the little ones of the flock. Surely he will make their habitation desolate over them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the call to hear the LORD’s counsel and purposes against Edom and Teman. His plans will be carried out.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s purposes as certain and effective. Both traditions commonly read the verse within its historical setting, noting its parallel in 50:45.

verses.text: The earth trembles at the noise of their fall; there is a cry, the noise which is heard in the Red Sea.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the earth trembling at the noise of Edom’s fall, with a cry heard at the Red Sea. The collapse is dramatic.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see poetic language for the magnitude of God’s judgment (compare 50:46). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as poetic and sober.

verses.text: Behold, he will come up and fly as the eagle, and spread out his wings against Bozrah. The heart of the mighty men of Edom at that day will be as the heart of a woman in her pangs.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see an attacker flying like an eagle against Bozrah, and Edom’s warriors gripped with fear. Strength turns to anguish.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the eagle image reversed: Edom nested high, but another eagle comes against it. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the oracle’s sober close.
